passages.title: Two Views of a Thunderstorm
passages.text:
Text 1

Milly pressed her nose to the cold window and grinned. Outside, the first fat drops of rain were beginning to fall, and far away the sky flickered with silver light. She loved storms more than anything. When the thunder finally rolled in, deep and grumbling like a giant turning over in his sleep, she counted the seconds between each flash and each boom, just as her grandfather had taught her. The garden had turned a strange, glowing green, and the puddles danced as the rain hammered down. Milly threw open the window and breathed in the sharp, clean smell of the wet earth. To her, a thunderstorm was better than any firework display, and entirely free.

Text 2

A thunderstorm is one of nature's most powerful and dangerous events. A single bolt of lightning is five times hotter than the surface of the sun and can split a tall tree in two in an instant. Every year, storms tear roofs from houses, flood streets and leave whole towns without power. People are warned to stay indoors, away from windows and tall trees, and never to shelter on open ground. Farmers watch anxiously as hail flattens their crops in minutes, and sailors far out at sea fear the towering waves that a storm can raise. For all its beauty, a thunderstorm demands respect, and those who ignore its dangers may pay a heavy price.
passages.source_note: Original work written for this pack (two contrasting passages on the same subject).

questions.stem: What do Text 1 and Text 2 have in common?

options.text: they are both written by children
they are both about a thunderstorm
they are both set at sea
they both give a weather forecast

questions.explanation: Both passages describe a thunderstorm, though in very different ways.

questions.stem: Although they feel very different, both writers agree that a thunderstorm is:

options.text: powerful and full of dramatic force

questions.explanation: Text 1 shows the rain hammering down; Text 2 stresses the storm's power -- both present it as a force to reckon with.

questions.stem: Which feature appears in both texts?

options.text: advice on how to measure a storm
the heavy rain or water that a storm brings

questions.explanation: Text 1 has hammering rain and puddles; Text 2 mentions floods, hail and towering waves -- both feature the water a storm brings.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between the two texts?

options.text: Text 1 is about rain and Text 2 about snow
Text 1 is a poem and Text 2 is a letter
Text 1 shows one child's feelings; Text 2 gives general facts
Text 1 is set at sea and Text 2 in a garden
Text 1 gives safety advice and Text 2 does not

questions.explanation: Text 1 follows Milly's personal delight; Text 2 sets out facts and warnings for everyone.

questions.stem: How does the purpose of the two texts differ?

options.text: Text 1 shares a personal love of storms; Text 2 alerts readers to their dangers
Text 1 sells a product; Text 2 tells a joke
Text 1 gives instructions; Text 2 asks questions
both simply read out a weather forecast
Text 1 teaches science; Text 2 tells a fairy tale

questions.explanation: Text 1 is written to share a feeling; Text 2 is written to inform and warn.

questions.stem: Text 2 gives facts and figures that Text 1 does not. This is because Text 2 is:

options.text: a personal story meant to entertain
an informative text meant to explain and advise
a poem meant to be sung
a private letter to a friend

questions.explanation: Facts such as the temperature of lightning belong to an informative text whose job is to explain and warn.

questions.stem: How do the two texts differ in who they are about?

options.text: both follow a girl called Milly
both follow a sailor at sea
Text 1 has no character and Text 2 follows a farmer
both are told by a grandfather
Text 1 follows a girl called Milly; Text 2 has no single character

questions.explanation: Text 1 centres on Milly; Text 2 speaks generally, with no main character.

questions.stem: How does the tone of Text 1 differ from that of Text 2?

options.text: Text 1 is angry, while Text 2 is cheerful
Text 1 is joyful and excited; Text 2 is grave and wary
Text 1 is calm, while Text 2 is playful

questions.explanation: Text 1 bubbles with excitement; Text 2 is measured and cautionary.

questions.stem: A reader is likely to feel very differently about storms after each text. Why?

options.text: Text 1 makes storms seem thrilling and beautiful; Text 2 makes them seem threatening and destructive
Text 1 makes them sound sad, while Text 2 makes them sound funny
both simply tell the reader to take shelter

questions.explanation: The two writers' opposite attitudes -- delight versus dread -- leave the reader feeling very differently.

questions.stem: Which words best sum up the feeling of each text?

options.text: fear in Text 1, joy in Text 2
wonder in Text 1, wariness in Text 2
sadness in Text 1, humour in Text 2

questions.explanation: Text 1 is full of wonder; Text 2 is full of caution.

questions.stem: What does Text 1 suggest about Milly?

options.text: she has never seen a storm before
she only wants to go to sleep
she finds storms thrilling rather than frightening

questions.explanation: She grins, throws open the window and calls the storm the best show there is -- she is thrilled, not scared.

questions.stem: Why does Milly count the seconds between each flash and boom?

options.text: because she is bored and restless
to time how long the rain will last
to work out how far away the storm is, as her grandfather taught her

questions.explanation: Counting between the flash and the thunder is a way of judging a storm's distance, a trick her grandfather taught her.

questions.stem: Why does the writer of Text 2 list so many different dangers?

options.text: to persuade readers to respect storms and stay safe
to prove that storms never really happen
to describe one particular storm from the past

questions.explanation: Piling up the dangers drives home the warning: storms deserve real respect.

questions.stem: Text 2 says sailors 'fear the towering waves'. This suggests that storms at sea are:

options.text: gentle and easy to sail through
especially dangerous, even for experienced sailors
never a real threat to ships
the safest place to be in a storm

questions.explanation: If even seasoned sailors fear them, storms at sea must be especially dangerous.

questions.stem: In Text 1 the thunder is 'deep and grumbling'. Here 'grumbling' means:
questions.explanation: 'Grumbling' here describes the low, rolling sound of distant thunder.

questions.stem: In Text 2, farmers watch 'anxiously' as hail falls. 'Anxiously' means:
questions.explanation: To watch 'anxiously' is to watch with worry -- the farmers fear for their crops.

questions.stem: Milly breathes in the 'sharp, clean smell of the wet earth'. Here 'sharp' describes a smell that is:
questions.explanation: A 'sharp' smell is a strong, fresh one -- here, the clean scent after rain.

questions.stem: Text 2 says a thunderstorm 'demands respect'. In this phrase, 'demands respect' means the storm:

options.text: must be treated with great care because of its power
wants to be admired for its beauty
needs to be studied at school

questions.explanation: To say something 'demands respect' is to say its power means we must treat it with serious care.

questions.stem: The writer of Text 1 compares the thunder to a giant turning over in his sleep in order to:

options.text: explain scientifically how thunder is made
make the huge noise feel friendly rather than frightening

questions.explanation: Likening the thunder to a sleepy giant makes its rumble feel cosy and harmless, matching Milly's delight.

questions.stem: Why does Text 2 tell readers exactly what NOT to do, such as sheltering under tall trees?

options.text: to describe the rules of a game
to show off the writer's knowledge
to give practical safety advice that could protect them

questions.explanation: The 'do nots' are safety advice, meant to keep readers out of danger.

questions.stem: Why does Text 1 end by calling the storm 'better than any firework display, and entirely free'?

options.text: to complain that fireworks are too expensive
to warn that storms are dangerous
to stress how much Milly delights in the storm, and at no cost
to explain how fireworks are made
to suggest that Milly is bored

questions.explanation: The comparison crowns Milly's delight: to her the storm is a dazzling show that costs nothing.

questions.stem: According to Text 2, a bolt of lightning is how much hotter than the surface of the sun?
questions.explanation: Text 2 states that lightning is 'five times hotter than the surface of the sun'.

questions.stem: In Text 1, who taught Milly to count the seconds during a storm?
questions.explanation: The text says she counted 'just as her grandfather had taught her'.

questions.stem: The writer says 'the puddles danced'. Which device is this?
questions.explanation: Puddles cannot really dance; giving them this action is personification.

questions.stem: 'like a giant turning over in his sleep' is an example of:
questions.explanation: It compares the thunder to a giant using the word 'like', which makes it a simile.
